summary: Defines the IPv6 addressing architecture: the addressing model, the text forms used to write addresses, the kinds of unicast, anycast, and multicast addresses, and which addresses a node must recognize as its own. It was replaced by RFC 4291.

eli5.summary: Every device on the internet needs an address, like a house number. This memo explains how the long new-style addresses are built, how to write them down, and the different kinds, such as one for a single house or one for a whole group.

questions: what is a link-local ipv6 address
subtitle: How 128-bit IPv6 addresses are written, what kinds exist, and which ones every node must recognize as its own.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needed a complete definition of what its 128-bit addresses look like, how to write them, and how to tell the different kinds apart.
tldr.mechanism: Addresses identify interfaces and come in three types (unicast, anycast, multicast), recognized by their leading bits, written as eight groups of hex with a compressing '::', and split into a prefix and a 64-bit interface identifier.
tldr.outcome: This RFC obsoleted RFC 2373 and is itself obsoleted by RFC 4291, so it documents an earlier version of the addressing architecture.

today: RFC 3513 obsoleted RFC 2373 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 4291, so RFC 4291 is the one to read for the current IPv6 addressing architecture.

sections.title: Address Types and the Addressing Model
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses are 128-bit identifiers for interfaces and sets of interfaces. There are three types:

  • Unicast: identifies a single interface; a packet goes to that interface.
  • Anycast: identifies a set of interfaces, usually on different nodes; a packet goes to one of them, the "nearest" by the routing protocols' measure of distance.
  • Multicast: identifies a set of interfaces; a packet goes to all of them.

There are no broadcast addresses in IPv6. Multicast takes over that function.

Addresses are assigned to interfaces, not nodes. Every interface MUST have at least one link-local unicast address, and may have several addresses of any type. A unicast address can be assigned to several physical interfaces if the implementation presents them to the internet layer as one interface, which is useful for load sharing. As in IPv4, a subnet prefix is associated with one link.

The type of an address is identified by its high-order bits. Anycast addresses come from the unicast space and cannot be told apart by looking at them. Anything that does not start with one of the listed prefixes MUST be treated as global unicast.

A node may view a unicast address as having no internal structure, or, like a simple host, as a subnet prefix of n bits followed by an interface ID of 128-n bits. Routers know more of the hierarchy, depending on their place in the routing hierarchy.

Unicast addresses are aggregatable with prefixes of arbitrary length, like IPv4 under CIDR. In IPv6, all zeros and all ones are legal values for any field unless specifically excluded.
sections.eli5:
An address can point to one house (unicast), to the closest house in a group (anycast), or to every house in a group at once (multicast). There is no shout-to-everyone option, because multicast covers that.

You can tell what kind of address you have by looking at how it starts, a bit like a phone number's area code.

sections.title: Writing Addresses and Prefixes
sections.content:
There are three conventional text forms:

  1. The preferred form is x:x:x:x:x:x:x:x, eight 16-bit pieces in hex, such as 1080:0:0:0:8:800:200C:417A. Leading zeros in a field may be dropped, but each field needs at least one digit.
  2. The compressed form uses :: for one or more groups of zeros. It can appear only once in an address, and may sit at the start or end. So FF01:0:0:0:0:0:0:101 becomes FF01::101, the loopback address becomes ::1 and the unspecified address becomes ::.
  3. A mixed form x:x:x:x:x:x:d.d.d.d ends in a dotted IPv4 address, for example ::FFFF:129.144.52.38.

Prefixes are written ipv6-address/prefix-length, as in CIDR notation. For instance the 60-bit prefix can be written 12AB:0:0:CD30::/60. Dropping trailing zeros inside a 16-bit field is not legal, so 12AB:0:0:CD3/60 is not the same prefix. A node address and its prefix can be combined, as in 12AB:0:0:CD30:123:4567:89AB:CDEF/60.
sections.eli5: An address is eight blocks of numbers and letters. To save writing, you can leave off zeros at the front of a block and replace one long run of all-zero blocks with two colons.

sections.title: Unicast Addresses in Detail
sections.content:
The interface identifier names an interface on a link and MUST be unique within a subnet prefix. For all unicast addresses except those starting with binary 000, it is 64 bits long and built in Modified EUI-64 format. When derived from an IEEE identifier, the universal/local "u" bit is inverted, so 1 means global scope and 0 means local scope. This makes hand-configured local identifiers simple, such as 1, 2, rather than 0200:0:0:1. Appendix A shows how to build them, including inserting 0xFF and 0xFE into a 48-bit MAC address.

Special unicast addresses:

  • Unspecified (::): never assigned to a node. It is used as the source address by a host that has not yet learned its address, and must not be a destination or be forwarded by routers.
  • Loopback (::1): lets a node send to itself; never assigned to a physical interface, and packets to it must never leave the node.
  • Global unicast: a global routing prefix, a subnet ID and an interface ID.
  • Embedded IPv4: the IPv4-compatible form carries an IPv4 address in the low 32 bits after 96 zero bits; the IPv4-mapped form has FFFF before the IPv4 address.
  • Link-local (FE80::/10): for a single link, used for things like automatic address configuration and neighbor discovery. Routers MUST NOT forward them.
  • Site-local (FEC0::/10): for use inside one site without a global prefix; routers MUST NOT forward them outside the site.
sections.eli5: Most of an address says which street you are on, and the last half says which house. Some special addresses mean 'I do not know my address yet', 'me', or 'only this street'.

sections.title: Anycast and Multicast
sections.content:
An anycast address is a unicast address assigned to more than one interface, and those nodes must be explicitly configured to know it. Because widespread use has little experience behind it, the RFC imposes two limits: an anycast address must not be the source of a packet, and it may be assigned only to routers, not hosts. Routers MUST support the predefined Subnet-Router anycast address, which is the subnet prefix with the interface ID set to zero.

A multicast address starts with 11111111, followed by a 4-bit flags field, a 4-bit scope and a 112-bit group ID. The three high flags are reserved and must be 0. The T flag is 0 for a permanent address assigned by IANA, 1 for a transient one. Scope values include 1 interface-local, 2 link-local, 4 admin-local, 5 site-local, 8 organization-local and E global.

A permanent group means the same thing at every scope: with group ID 101 for NTP servers, FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:101 is all NTP servers on the sender's link and FF0E:0:0:0:0:0:0:101 is all NTP servers in the internet. Multicast addresses must not be used as a source address, and routers must not forward a packet beyond its scope.

Predefined groups include all nodes (FF01::1 and FF02::1) and all routers (FF01::2, FF02::2 and FF05::2). The solicited-node address takes the low-order 24 bits of a unicast or anycast address and appends them to FF02:0:0:0:0:1:FF00::/104. A node MUST join the solicited-node group for each of its unicast and anycast addresses.
sections.eli5: Anycast is shouting 'any helper, come here' and the closest one answers. Multicast is a group chat where everyone in the group gets the message, and the 'scope' decides how far the message is allowed to travel.

sections.title: A Node's Required Addresses
sections.content:
A host MUST recognize as its own: its link-local address for each interface, any other configured unicast and anycast addresses, the loopback address, the all-nodes multicast addresses, the solicited-node address for each unicast and anycast address, and the multicast addresses of all other groups it belongs to.

A router MUST recognize all of those, plus the Subnet-Router anycast addresses for the interfaces it routes on, any other anycast addresses it has been configured with, and the all-routers multicast addresses.
sections.eli5: Every computer has to answer to a list of names, such as its own, 'everybody' and any clubs it joined. Routers answer to a few extra names, like 'any router'.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The security section is brief: IPv6 addressing documents do not have any direct impact on Internet infrastructure security, and authentication of IPv6 packets is defined elsewhere (RFC 2402).

The IANA section replaces the older address space table. Global Unicast is allocated from prefix 001, which is 1/8 of the space, and IANA is told to limit unicast allocation to that range for now. The rest of the global unicast space, about 85% of the total, is reserved for future definition. Link-local and site-local each take 1/1024, and multicast takes 1/256.

Appendix B lists changes from RFC 2373. Among them, interface identifiers must now be unique within a subnet prefix rather than on a link, the site-local subnet ID became 54 bits, and the multicast scope values were described.
sections.eli5: Addresses themselves do not make the internet safer or less safe. The registry keeps most of the address space in reserve for later.

items.label: Unspecified
items.desc: All zeros; absence of an address.

items.label: Global unicast
items.desc: Treated as global unicast unless redefined.
